label: L4
title: Class 4: Leading Change at OCP, from Cognitive Biases to Business Steering
brief: Class 4 opens with Boston's school-bus optimization (about \$5M of routing savings, ~50 buses off the road, up to \$14M more from start times) to argue that effective solutions are not enough without cultural adaptation, and then reads the OCP case through finance, production, formal-organization, political and data lenses. Cognitive biases (confirmation, anchoring, framing, sunk cost, functional fixedness, pain-avoiding denial, social conformity, theory-induced blindness, survivorship) and Kegan and Lahey's immunity-to-change map explain why sound studies get resisted, as with the slurry-pipeline feasibility study. At the end of 2006 OCP had negative net equity of −16.2 Bn MAD, a pension 'ticking bomb', a falling rock share, a siloed volume-oriented bureaucracy and a recruitment moratorium; Kotter's eight steps structure the response, from urgency and a vision of cost, capacity and agility leadership to quick wins such as a +30% price increase in March 2007 and a debut US\$1.85bn bond. The shift from the rock-and-acid S-curve to a fertilizer S-curve, which has to avoid the identity, architecture and collaboration traps, quadrupled fertilizer capacity and lifted world fertilizer market share from 11% to 27% between 2007 and 2025. Business steering gave the company one global view through a multi-period MILP (about 600,000 constraints, 60,000 binaries) whose shadow prices show that an incremental deal must be judged on $m_i-(Ae_i)^\top y$ rather than its unit margin, worth about US\$490M in 2020. Digital manufacturing extends this from physical flows to data flows on one shared platform run by mixed digital-process teams.
kp: Effective solutions are not enough without cultural adaptation: Boston's bus optimizer saved ~\$5M but needed people to make it work.
OCP is read through five lenses: finance, production, formal organization, political and data.

Biases that block change: confirmation, anchoring, framing, sunk cost, functional fixedness, pain-avoiding denial, social conformity, theory-induced blindness; survivorship bias learns only from successes.
Immunity to change: actual commitment → behaviour that undermines it → hidden competing commitment → big assumption held as fact.
End-2006 OCP: assets 28.3 Bn MAD against liabilities of 44.5 Bn MAD (net equity −16.2), pension fund a 'ticking bomb', no recruitment 1985–2006.
Kotter: change agents fail when they rely mostly on reason and structure and neglect human, political and symbolic elements.
Change levers: state office → limited company; volume royalties → profitability-based dividends; 'sell all you can produce' → 'produce only what you can sell'.
Three traps stymie reinvention: identity, architecture and collaboration.
Business steering: one multi-period MILP over the whole chain; shadow prices value capacity, so an order is worth $m_i-(Ae_i)^\top y$, not $m_i$.
Digital manufacturing: from physical to data flows, each plant modelled on its own data with one global optimum, SC manager paired with a data scientist.

topics.x: Boston Public Schools' bus problem (~200 schools, ~25,000 students, ~700 buses, \$116M a year or 12% of BPS funds) was solved with efficient optimization: +\$5M of routing savings reinvested in education, ~50 buses off the road, and up to \$14M more from start-time selection. Joi Ito's point is that technology can make systems fairer but will not succeed without human help. The class then examines OCP through five lenses: finance, production, formal organization, political and data.

Kahneman and Munger supply the catalogue: confirmation bias, anchoring, framing, sunk cost (choices that justify previous decisions), pain-avoiding psychological denial, social conformity, theory-induced blindness (clinging to outdated paradigms) and functional fixedness ('if the only tool you have is a hammer...'). The Simons attention videos show how much we miss, and survivorship bias means learning only from successful trials. At OCP, 'taking production to another site was not an option' until a study showed that moving ammonia production to Jorf removed the risk and raised profit.

Kegan and Lahey's map has four columns: the actual commitment, what the person does or does not do instead, the hidden competing commitment that protects against a feared outcome, and the big assumption held as fact. In the heart-patient example, skipping medication protects against feeling old. At OCP, managers formally committed to lowering costs through the slurry pipeline introduced wrong assumptions and launched a competing study, protecting a big assumption that their leadership rested only on technical competence.

topics.n: OCP's change imperative and Kotter's eight steps
topics.x: By 2006 OCP had an export fee that was an inefficient incentive, a mine-versus-chemicals quality battle, a 'phosphate sells itself' sales culture, seniority-based promotion, a 1985–2006 recruitment moratorium, a pension 'ticking bomb' and negative net equity, while the market moved from rock to fertilizers. Kotter's steps organise the response: urgency, a coalition, a vision of cost, capacity (×2 mining, ×3 fertilizer) and agility leadership, then quick wins such as a +30% price increase in March 2007 (against +3% initially recommended), a strategic 2009 shutdown backed by staff, and a US\$1.85bn debut bond. Change agents fail when they neglect human, political and symbolic elements.

topics.n: The second S-curve and the three traps
topics.x: OCP's first S-curve was rock and acid; the second, from 2006, standard fertilizers, with a shift from volume maximization, centralized silos and seniority to 'produce what you can sell', decentralized collaboration, merit and a growth mindset. Raffaelli's three traps describe what blocks such reinvention: identity (who we are = the past product), architecture (new teams run on old structures and incentives) and collaboration (silos between teams at different phases of the S-curve). Results: an \$8bn Phase 1 CAPEX program, fertilizer capacity 4 → 16 MT, world fertilizer share 11% → 27% (2007–2025), revenues \$2.5bn (2005) → \$12.3bn (2025).

topics.n: Business steering: one global MILP and shadow prices
topics.x: Business steering merged mining and chemicals into one industrial department beside a steering unit, and modelled the whole chain (8 mines, 22 rock grades, 9 acid qualities, 43 fertilizer grades, 4 ports) as a multi-period MILP maximising revenue minus extraction, treatment, sourcing and transport costs; a daily model has ~600,000 constraints and ~500,000 variables (60,000 binary). LP duality explains the 'layer for customer X': forcing one unit of product $i$ turns the right-hand side into $b-Ae_i$, so profit changes by $m_i-(Ae_i)^\top y$. Products with high unit margins can have negative shadow prices; the estimated value unlocked was about US\$490M in 2020.

topics.n: Digital manufacturing and the ONE platform
topics.x: Business steering focused on physical flows, used the same generic data for every plant and put the supply-chain manager at the centre. Digital manufacturing focuses on data flows: each plant is modelled on its own data as modular bricks with one global optimum, SC managers are paired with data scientists, mixed digital-process teams are accountable for performance, and digital becomes a way of working. Jorf Lasfar's ONE platform replaces per-unit tech and data with a common database, an AA & AI factory and Gen AI orchestration, echoing Bezos's 2002 service-interface mandate.

cards.f: What does the Boston school-bus case teach about analytics?
cards.b: Efficient optimization saved ~\$5M in routing (reinvested in education, ~50 buses off the road) with up to \$14M more possible from start times, but effective solutions are not enough without cultural adaptation.
cards.x: The algorithm was the easy part; adoption was not.

cards.f: Name the five lenses used to analyse OCP.
cards.b: Finance, production, formal organization, political and data.
cards.x: Each lens surfaces a different obstacle to change.

cards.b: Confirmation bias: searching for, interpreting, favouring and recalling information that supports prior beliefs. Anchoring: giving disproportionate weight to the first piece of information.
cards.x: One filters the evidence; the other overweights the starting point.

cards.b: Theory-induced blindness: clinging to old paradigms that have outlived their validity. Sunk cost: making choices as a way to justify previous decisions.
cards.x: The first protects a belief; the second protects a past decision.

cards.b: Learning only from successful trials; a related statistical bias is random-incidence (sampling) bias.
cards.x: The failures that would change your conclusion are missing from the sample.

cards.f: What did the Safi ammonia study show?
cards.b: Managers held that moving production to another site was not an option; a study showed that moving ammonia production to Jorf not only removed the risk but generated more profit.
cards.x: A frame ruled out the better option before anyone analysed it.

cards.f: The four columns of the immunity-to-change map?
cards.b: Actual commitment; doing / not doing instead; hidden competing commitment; big assumption.
cards.x: The big assumption is held as fact, which is why it stays invisible.

cards.f: Immunity map of the slurry-pipeline managers?
cards.b: Commitment: lower group costs by supporting the pipeline. Instead: wrong assumptions in the feasibility study and a competing study to reinforce NO-GO. Competing commitment: not appearing incompetent. Big assumption: their leadership role is justified only by technical competence.
cards.x: The resistance protected status, not the business case.

cards.f: OCP's balance sheet at the end of 2006?
cards.b: Assets of 28.3 Bn MAD (cash 11.4 + other assets 16.9) against 44.5 Bn MAD of liabilities including the pension liability, giving net equity of −16.2 Bn MAD.
cards.x: Negative equity made the urgency undeniable.

cards.f: Kotter's warning about why change agents fail?
cards.b: They rely mostly on reason and structure while neglecting human, political and symbolic elements.
cards.x: A correct plan still needs a coalition, a story and quick wins.

cards.f: Name OCP's main constraint → change-lever moves.
cards.b: State office → limited company; internally managed pension fund → outsourced management and a stronger balance sheet; volume-based royalties → profitability-based dividends; 'sell all you can produce' → 'produce only what you can sell'; volume bureaucracy → value-oriented, decentralized company.
cards.x: Each lever removes an incentive that rewarded volume over value.

cards.b: A +30% $/t price increase achieved in March 2007 (the initial mindset recommended +3%), and a US\$1.85bn debut bond (US\$1.25bn 10-year at 5.625%, US\$600M 30-year at 6.875%).
cards.x: Quick wins signal externally and internally that the vision is real.

cards.f: The three traps that stymie organizational innovation?
cards.b: Identity (who we are = the product that defined past success), architecture (innovation teams run on the structures and incentives of established products), collaboration (silos between teams at different S-curve phases).
cards.x: Each trap is a reason the second S-curve gets starved by the first.

cards.f: Size of the business-steering MILP (daily model)?
cards.b: About 600,000 constraints and 500,000 variables, 60,000 of them binary, covering 21 mines, 5 beneficiation units, 10 phosphoric acid lines and 15 fertilizer lines.
cards.x: One global optimum instead of each department optimising its own piece.

cards.f: Shadow-price rule for an incremental order of product $i$?
cards.b: Decide on $m_i-(Ae_i)^\top y^*$: the unit margin minus the capacity the order consumes, valued at the optimal dual prices, not on $m_i$ alone.
cards.x: A high unit margin can still destroy global margin.

cards.b: Steering: physical flows, plant by plant, supply-chain manager at the centre, digital as technology. Digital manufacturing: data flows, one global optimum, SC manager plus data scientist in mixed teams accountable for performance, digital as a way of working.
cards.x: The second is run by operational teams and driven by field needs.

quiz.q: What share of Boston Public Schools' funds went to school buses?
quiz.e: The slide gives \$116M per year, rising, or 12% of BPS funds. \$14M is the potential saving from start-time selection, not the bus budget.

quiz.q: Which bias is defined as 'making choices as a way to justify previous decisions'?
quiz.e: Sunk cost justifies past decisions. Anchoring is overweighting the first piece of information, which is about the starting point, not past commitments.

quiz.q: What is the first of Kotter's eight steps?
quiz.e: Urgency comes first; at OCP it rested on the pension 'ticking bomb' and negative equity. Quick wins come only after a coalition and a vision exist.

o: Leaders and employees tie 'who we are' to the product or service that defined past success
Innovation teams are made to run on the structures and incentives of established products
Teams at different phases of the S-curve fail to trust or learn from one another
Employees copy each other's beliefs to fit in
quiz.e: Identity is about self-image tied to the old product. The second option is the architecture trap and the third the collaboration trap.

quiz.q: OCP's revenues went from \$2.5bn (2005) to \$12.3bn (2025). Roughly what multiple is that?
quiz.e: 12.3 / 2.5 ≈ 4.9. 2.8× is the 2005–2012 step (\$6.9bn / \$2.5bn), not the full period.

quiz.q: At the end of 2006 OCP had 28.3 Bn MAD of assets and 44.5 Bn MAD of liabilities. What was its net equity?
quiz.e: Net equity = assets − liabilities = 28.3 − 44.5 = −16.2 Bn MAD, as shown on the slide. Adding the two (72.8) confuses the balance-sheet identity.

quiz.q: Bus costs of \$116M are 12% of BPS funds. What total BPS budget does that imply?
quiz.e: 116 / 0.12 ≈ 967, so about \$0.97bn. 116 × 1.2 = \$139M and 116 × 12 = \$1.4bn are the usual slips of multiplying instead of dividing.

quiz.q: In the slurry-pipeline immunity map, which item is the 'big assumption'?
o: Their leadership role is justified only by their technical competency
Lower costs within the group by supporting the slurry pipeline
Introduce wrong assumptions into the feasibility study
quiz.e: The big assumption is the belief held as fact that drives the fear. 'Not appearing incompetent' is the hidden competing commitment it produces, the tempting wrong answer.

quiz.q: Suppose OCP's ask price was \$400/t. How much more per ton did the achieved +30% increase bring than the initially recommended +3%?
quiz.e: 400 × 0.30 − 400 × 0.03 = 120 − 12 = \$108/t. \$120 is the whole increase, ignoring the +3% baseline being compared against.

quiz.q: Which change lever replaced the 'sell all you can produce' mentality?
o: A margin-optimization approach: 'produce only what you can sell'
Profitability-based dividends instead of volume-based royalties
Conversion from a state office into a limited company
quiz.e: The volume-based 5-year rolling plan was replaced by margin optimization. Dividends replaced royalties, a different constraint (the government incentive), not the sales mindset.

quiz.q: Which key success factor belongs to OCP's second S-curve?
o: Using analytics to optimize product mix: 'produce what you can sell'
High capacity utilization and 'sell all you produce'
quiz.e: The second S-curve uses analytics and market intelligence. Capacity utilization, reactive maintenance and seniority all describe the first, volume-driven S-curve.

quiz.q: Rock capacity went from 30 to 49 MT and fertilizer capacity from 4 to 16 MT (2007–2025). Which statement is right?
o: Fertilizer capacity quadrupled while rock capacity rose about 63%
Rock capacity quadrupled while fertilizer rose about 63%
quiz.e: 16 / 4 = 4× and 49 / 30 ≈ 1.63, i.e. +63%. The growth went downstream into fertilizers, matching the shift to the second S-curve.

quiz.q: Which feature belongs to digital manufacturing rather than business steering?
o: Each plant modelled on its own data as modular bricks, with one global optimum
The same generic data used for every plant
The supply-chain manager as the single central role
quiz.e: Digital manufacturing models each plant on its own data and pairs SC managers with data scientists. Generic data, a single central SC manager and digital-as-technology all describe business steering.

quiz.q: OCP raised US\$1.25bn at 5.625% and US\$600M at 6.875%. What is the amount-weighted average coupon?

An extra ton of product $i$ has unit margin $m_i$ = \$50 and uses 2 units of resource 1 (shadow price \$20) and 1 unit of resource 2 (shadow price \$15). Using the class's rule, what is the effect on global margin?
o: −\$5 per ton: reject, it lowers global margin
+\$50 per ton: accept, the unit margin is positive
quiz.e: $m_i-(Ae_i)^\top y = 50 - (2\cdot20 + 1\cdot15) = 50 - 55 = -5$. Looking at $m_i$ alone (+\$50) is exactly the 'customer X' mistake; −\$55 forgets to add back the margin.

quiz.q: In the shadow-price derivation, why does profit change by exactly $-(Ae_i)^\top y$ when one unit of product $i$ is forced?
o: For a small enough perturbation of $b$ the optimal dual solution does not change, so the dual objective moves from $b^\top y$ to $(b-Ae_i)^\top y$
Because forcing a product makes the primal infeasible
Because the 60,000 binary variables fix the optimal basis
quiz.e: Forcing $e_i$ turns the constraints into $Ax\le b-Ae_i$; with the dual optimum unchanged, the optimal value shifts by $(b-Ae_i)^\top y - b^\top y = -(Ae_i)^\top y$. $Ae_i$ is the resource use of product $i$, which is not zero.

quiz.q: In the Q3 2011 chart, special phosphoric acid (ACP spéciaux) had a unit margin of about 715 $/t and a shadow price of about −57 $/t. What does that mean?
o: Each extra ton lowers global margin by about \$57 despite the high unit margin, because it consumes capacity that is worth more elsewhere
Each extra ton raises global margin by about \$715
Each extra ton raises global margin by about \$658 (715 − 57)
It should be prioritised because it has one of the highest unit margins
quiz.e: The shadow price already nets the unit margin against the capacity it uses, so the marginal effect on global margin is −57 $/t. Subtracting 57 from 715 double-counts the margin.

written.q: OCP managers resisted the slurry-pipeline project by introducing wrong assumptions into its feasibility study. Diagnose this resistance with the immunity-to-change framework and at least two cognitive biases from class, then propose how a change leader could address it using Kotter's eight steps.
written.m: Immunity map: the stated commitment was to lower group costs by supporting the slurry pipeline. What they did instead was introduce wrong assumptions into the study and launch a competing study 'behind the scene' to reinforce a NO-GO decision. The hidden competing commitment was not appearing incompetent; the big assumption, held as fact, was that their leadership role was justified only by their technical competency, with fears of looking incompetent and losing their position. Biases: confirmation bias (searching for and favouring evidence for NO-GO), sunk cost (justifying the existing transport set-up), theory-induced blindness (clinging to an old paradigm) and pain-avoiding denial (avoiding the uncomfortable regardless of value). The Safi ammonia case shows the same pattern: 'not an option' until a study showed moving to Jorf removed the risk and raised profit. Kotter: establish urgency with the facts (negative net equity of −16.2 Bn MAD, pension 'ticking bomb', shift from rock to fertilizers); build a coalition that includes the technical leaders so their status is tied to the new project; state a vision (cost, capacity and agility leadership); communicate it; empower people; create quick wins; consolidate and institutionalise. The class's warning applies: change agents fail when they rely on reason and structure and neglect human, political and symbolic elements, so the leader must test the big assumption, for instance by giving these managers visible roles in delivering the pipeline.
k: Four columns filled correctly: commitment, undermining behaviour, competing commitment, big assumption
Big assumption = leadership justified only by technical competency
At least two biases named and defined correctly
Link to OCP facts (pension bomb, negative equity, market shift) as urgency
Kotter's steps applied in a sensible order
Human/political/symbolic elements, not only reason and structure

written.q: Explain how OCP's business-steering programme used LP duality to change commercial decisions. Give the perturbation argument, interpret the 'layer for customer X' episode and the shadow-price chart, and explain why an organizational redesign was needed for the model to have impact.
written.m: Primal: $\max m^\top x$ s.t. $Ax\le b$, $x\ge0$; dual: $\min b^\top y$ s.t. $A^\top y\ge m$, $y\ge0$. Forcing one extra unit of product $i$ ($x+e_i$) gives $\max m^\top x + m_i$ s.t. $Ax\le b-Ae_i$. For a small perturbation the dual optimum is unchanged, so the optimal value of the rest changes by $(b-Ae_i)^\top y - b^\top y = -(Ae_i)^\top y$, and the net effect of the order is $m_i-(Ae_i)^\top y$. Commercial decisions should use this, not $m_i$. In the customer-X story a miner pointed to a layer and bulldozers brought specially for one order: 'we are losing money on this deal'. The shadow-price chart shows the same thing in numbers: special acid had a high unit margin (~715 $/t) but a negative shadow price (~−57 $/t), so each extra ton lowered global margin, while TSP was positive (~+90 $/t). The model itself is a multi-period MILP over the whole chain (revenue minus extraction, physical and chemical treatment, sourcing and transport costs, subject to demand, extraction, treatment and contract constraints), with ~600,000 constraints and ~500,000 variables (60,000 binary) for a daily model. It only mattered because the organization changed: mining and chemicals had a 'never-ending battle over quality' and sales believed 'phosphate sells itself'; merging them into one industrial department and adding a business-steering unit under executive management created one owner for the global optimum. The estimated value unlocked was about US\$490M in 2020.
k: Perturbation to $b-Ae_i$ and unchanged dual optimum
Customer-X interpretation: capacity consumed has an opportunity cost
Reads the chart: high unit margin, negative shadow price
Reorganization: industrial department + business steering, one global optimum
